## The picture

Fix a height $t$ on the critical strip and a real part $\sigma$. The partial sums

$$
S_k(s) = \sum_{n=1}^{k} n^{-s}, \qquad k = 1, 2, 3, \dots
$$

don't converge as $k \to \infty$ — but plotted in the complex plane, they don't wander randomly either. They spiral: each new term rotates the running total by a bit more than the last (the phase of $n^{-s}$ is $-t \log n$, so consecutive terms rotate relative to each other by a shrinking angle), and the whole path winds in toward a fixed center. By December 2024 I had a name for this — the spiral picture — and enough of a feel for it to know it was worth pinning down exactly, not just admiring.

## Pinning it down

Treat the real and imaginary parts of the partial sum as right-rule Riemann sum approximations to integrals, $I_\Re(N) = \int_0^N x^{-\sigma}\cos(-t\log x)\,dx$ and $I_\Im(N)$ likewise with $\sin$. Integration by parts on both, then a little algebra with

$$
\alpha = \frac{1}{\sqrt{t^2+(1-\sigma)^2}}, \qquad \omega = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{1-\sigma}{\sqrt{t^2+(1-\sigma)^2}}\right),
$$

collapses them to a closed form:

$$
I_\Re(N) = \alpha N^{1-\sigma}\cos(-t\log N + \omega), \qquad I_\Im(N) = \alpha N^{1-\sigma}\sin(-t\log N + \omega).
$$

That's exactly a spiral — $\Sigma(N) = I_\Re(N) + iI_\Im(N)$ traces a curve centered at the origin with radius $\alpha N^{1-\sigma}$, shrinking as $N$ grows for any $\sigma > 1$ and just barely failing to shrink at $\sigma = 1$, which is the boundary where $\zeta$'s defining series itself stops converging. The picture isn't a metaphor; it's a literal consequence of integrating an oscillating power function.

## Where the real center is

$\Sigma(N)$ is an approximation to the partial sum, not the partial sum itself, so define the difference $\mu_1^N(s) = \zeta_1^N(s) - \Sigma(N)$ and its limit $\mu(s) = \lim_{N\to\infty}\mu_1^N(s)$. This $\mu(s)$ — not the origin — is the *actual* center the true partial sums spiral around; $\Sigma(N)$ only nails the shape and radius of the spiral, not quite where it's centered. Getting a good, finite, computable estimate of $\mu(s)$ turns out to matter a great deal later — it's the seed of the pre-tail construction in [Chapter 4](../pre-tail-and-tail/index.qmd) — but the qualitative picture is already the whole point of this chapter: $M = \lfloor t/\pi \rfloor$, close to where the phase function's stationary point sits, is a natural place to stop and read off where that center is, which is exactly why the truncation

$$
f(s) = \sum_{n=1}^{M} n^{-s} + \tfrac12 (M+1)^{-s}
$$

that recurs throughout the rest of this project uses that specific cutoff.

The question that makes this more than a curiosity: *where* does the center sit? At a real, known zero of $\zeta$ — one of the actual heights $t$ where $\zeta(\tfrac12+it)=0$ — and exactly on the critical line, the center is the origin. Nudge $\sigma$ away from $\tfrac12$, height held fixed, and the same spiral winds toward some other point entirely, not zero.

## Try it

Pick a known zero from the list below, then drag the $\sigma$-offset fader off the critical line and watch the final point (the colored dot) leave the origin.

```{=html}
<iframe src="spiral_gauge.html" style="width:100%; aspect-ratio: 3/4; max-width: 780px; border: 1px solid #d6dce3; border-radius: 6px; display:block; margin: 1.5rem auto;" loading="lazy"></iframe>
```

Each point along the path is a running total of $n^{-s}$; the color goes from muted to full as $n$ runs from $1$ to the displayed cutoff. The path is drawn a few multiples past $M$ purely so the winding is legible to the eye — the small diamond marks where $f(s)$ is actually evaluated. The fifteen preset heights are the first fifteen known nontrivial zeros of $\zeta$, so "locked" at $\sigma = 0.5$ isn't a simulation — it's the real function, doing the real thing.
